analysis.file_name: Risk Premium in Pictures - Why have higher bond yields not derailed the equity rally.pdf
analysis.title: Risk Premium in Pictures: The Great Disconnect, Why Have Higher Bond Yields Not Derailed the Equity Rally?
key_insights: Higher bond yields have not hurt equities in 2026. The report's chart pack compares 2026 changes in government bond yields with 2026 local-currency equity returns across 17 markets, and frames the question as why the equity rally survived the yield rise.

In the US, the cost of equity has risen in 2026 alongside the 10-year Treasury yield. The report's decomposition of the change in the US equity risk premium (ERP) runs from 365 bps at the start of the year to 323 bps now: yield -113 bps, market rally -26 bps, earnings +97 bps.
Earnings growth is what has offset the higher yield. Earnings add 97 bps to the ERP in 2026, against a 113 bps drag from yields and a 26 bps drag from the market's own rise.
The US ERP is 3.2% as of 29/09/2026, against a 4.2% average, a 1.3% minimum and a 7.7% maximum. SG calls it closer to the critical threshold of 3%.

The model inputs are earnings growth of 32% in 2026e and 16% in both 2027e and 2028e, medium-term growth of 9.0%, long-term growth of 5.5%, a 10-year bond yield of 5.2%, an internal rate of return of 8.5% and a 40% payout ratio.

A US ERP below 3% has historically been difficult. The ERP has stayed below 3% less than 10% of the time since 1990, US equities are flat over the following 12 months at sub-3% ERP, and at lower ERP they underperform Treasuries.
Against corporate credit, US equity valuation relative to investment-grade bonds is near its historical average, and US equities offer better value than US high-yield credit.

A 10-year Treasury yield at 6% would be a headwind for US equities. SG's sensitivity charts show US equity downside at yields of 5.50%, 5.75%, 6.00% and 6.25% if there are no further earnings upgrades, and the 2027e and 2028e earnings upgrades needed to hold the ERP at 3%.
The report also charts the convexity of US and UK 10-year government bonds. The chart carries a 'Data as of 01/03/2024' label, so its data date differs from the rest of the pack.
earnings_insights: SG's ERP model uses earnings growth estimates of 32% for 2026e and 16% each for 2027e and 2028e. The report does not say whether these are consensus or SG forecasts, or whether they are reported or adjusted.
Earnings added 97 bps to the US equity risk premium in 2026, which offset most of the 113 bps drag from higher yields.
The report says 2027e and 2028e earnings upgrades would be needed to keep the ERP at 3% if the 10-year yield rises toward 6%.
risk_factors: The US equity risk premium is near the 3% threshold, below which it has historically been difficult for US equities.
A 10-year Treasury yield at 6% without further earnings upgrades would be a headwind for US equities.
At sub-3% ERP, US equities have been flat over the following 12 months and have underperformed Treasuries.
The rally depends on high earnings growth (32% in 2026e, 16% in 2027e and 2028e), so any shortfall removes the offset to higher yields.
charts_described: Slide 2 compares changes in government bond yields in 2026 (in bps) with 2026 local-currency equity performance across 17 markets, including the USA, Japan, Korea, Taiwan, China, India and several European markets. The text gives no values.

Slide 3 charts the US cost of equity against the UST yield in 2026, with the cost of equity axis at 7.4% to 8.6%, and a decomposition of the 2026 change in ERP: 365 start, -113 yield, -26 market, 97 earnings, 323 final (bps).
Slide 4 plots the US equity risk premium since 1990 with 'Danger zone' and 'Irrational exuberance' (dotcoms, early 2000) zones. Data as of 29/09/2026.

Slide 5 shows the distribution of the US ERP (below 3% less than 10% of the time since 1990), 12-month US equity performance by ERP level (flat at sub-3% ERP), and 12-month US equity performance relative to Treasuries (underperformance at lower ERP).
Slide 6 charts US equity valuation relative to investment-grade credit (near historical average) and to high-yield credit (equities offer better value).

Slide 7 charts US equity downside, and the earnings upgrades needed to hold the ERP at 3%, for 10-year yields of 5.50% to 6.25%, plus the convexity of US and UK 10-year government bonds. The slide is labelled 'Data as of 01/03/2024'.

tension_points.bull_case: Earnings growth has offset the higher yield: it adds 97 bps to the ERP in 2026 against a 113 bps drag from yields. Earnings growth is modelled at 32% in 2026e and 16% in 2027e and 2028e. US equity valuation versus investment-grade credit is near its historical average, and equities offer better value than US high-yield credit.
tension_points.bear_case: The US ERP of 3.2% is close to the 3% threshold. The ERP has stayed below 3% less than 10% of the time since 1990, US equities are flat over the following 12 months at sub-3% ERP, and at lower ERP they underperform Treasuries. A 10-year yield at 6% would be a headwind.
tension_points.what_invalidates: The 10-year Treasury yield rising toward 6% (charted at 5.50% to 6.25%) without further 2027e and 2028e earnings upgrades, or the US ERP falling below 3%.
